name: Capitalism
summary: Capitalism is an economic system in which most means of production are privately owned and production and prices are guided by markets, competition and the profit motive. Its defenders, Hessen and Adam Smith among them, hold that self-interested exchange under secure property rights, with a state limited to defence, justice and a few public works, produces widely shared prosperity, and they oppose tariffs, monopoly privileges and state direction of investment. The sources named leave most questions of society, culture and foreign policy open.
scope: The mainstream pro-market account of capitalism as its defining sources give it: Hessen's Concise Encyclopedia of Economics entry (economic individualism, private property, self-interest, a state that protects individual rights), Britannica's entry (private ownership of the means of production, markets, profit motive) and Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, which both name as the founding statement of the system. It excludes the critics' account (Marx, Piketty), state capitalism, and the stricter libertarian and anarcho-capitalist wing. Questions of culture, religion, family and foreign policy lie largely outside it, so most such statements are null.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Smith names defending society against other independent societies as the first duty of the sovereign, and says only a standing army can perpetuate a civilised country.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Smith's Book I makes the division of labour the source of the growth in the productive powers of labour; Hessen treats specialisation as a strength of capitalism that Marx promised to end.

abolish-ip.rationale: Smith says a temporary monopoly granted to a new machine's inventor or a book's author can be vindicated, though he says it should end at a set term.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Smith treats money as the instrument of commerce that exchange under the division of labour requires, and Hessen lists the abolition of money among the sweeping promises Marx made.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Smith's account of the wealth of nations treats wages, profit and rent as the component parts of price, with labour hired for wages as a basic feature of commercial society.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Private ownership of the means of production, land included, is the defining feature in Britannica, and Hessen makes the right to own private property its basic premise.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Smith's Book V argues that accumulated public debts have ruined states and have scarcely ever been paid off fairly, which counts against running large deficits.

ban-cartels.rationale: Smith says no law that could be executed consistently with liberty and justice can prevent tradesmen meeting to raise prices, only that law should not facilitate it, and Hessen argues antitrust law has often suppressed price cutting.

ban-interest.rationale: Smith says that where interest has been prohibited by law the prohibition has increased the evil of usury, and he treats payment for the use of money as proper.

bound-labor.rationale: Smith calls the laws that restrain a poor man from settling where he chooses an evident violation of natural liberty and justice, and defends a workman's liberty to work where he thinks proper.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Hessen holds that the benefits of capitalism were widely diffused, turning luxuries into necessities and promising Smith's universal opulence; Britannica cites the sustained growth of productive forces under it.

central-planning.rationale: Smith holds that no statesman or council can direct how private people employ their capitals, and Britannica contrasts the market with command systems as distinct ways of organising an economy.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Smith argues that the monopoly of colonial trade hurts the mother country's own people for the benefit of a few merchants, rejecting government of colonies for the ruling country's economic gain.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Hessen dismisses the labelling of prosperity as mindless materialism as a repackaged old criticism of capitalism.

corporate-influence.rationale: Smith warns that proposals for commercial regulation from merchants and manufacturers come from men whose interest is to deceive and oppress the public, and Hessen notes organised recipients keep special favours.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: Smith's Book IV rejects the physiocratic view that land is the only source of a nation's wealth, treating labour, manufactures and commerce as productive.

delink-world-market.rationale: Smith argues that freedom of trade between nations enriches all of them, so a poor country ending its trade ties with rich ones runs against his system.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Smith's Book IV chapter on colonies condemns the colonial monopoly that confines the colonies' trade to the mother country.

family-wage.rationale: Smith holds it is but equity that those who feed, clothe and lodge the whole people should have enough of their own produce to be tolerably well fed, clothed and lodged, and notes wages must support a family.

farm-price-support.rationale: Smith criticises the corn bounty and other measures that interfere with the price of corn, and argues for unrestrained freedom of the corn trade.

free-trade.rationale: Smith's Book IV argues that freedom of trade between nations serves every nation's wealth, and Hessen criticises tariff protection for letting protected producers stagnate.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: Smith says commerce ought naturally to be among nations a bond of union and friendship, and blames the mercantile restrictions on it for making it a source of discord.

land-redistribution.rationale: Hessen makes secure private property the basic premise of the system, and he contrasts it with socialist doctrines that deny inalienable property rights.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Hessen presents economic individualism as the system of free, competing producers and Britannica defines capitalism as production and pricing driven by market forces; Smith's 'system of natural liberty' recommends leaving economic decisions to the market.

national-church-status.rationale: Smith argues that the state should treat all sects impartially, with every man choosing his own religion, and describes an established church's clergy as a privileged incorporation.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Hessen defends capitalism as the system that delivers prosperity and rejects the socialist alternative, so he denies that capitalism is an unsound basis for society.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Smith assigns the sovereign three duties (defence, justice, and public works and institutions no individual could profitably maintain), which goes beyond protecting people from physical violence; Hessen likewise has the state protect rights generally.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Smith attacks exclusive companies and monopolies granted to merchants, and Hessen says special favours to business became entrenched at consumers' expense.

people-in-arms.rationale: Smith argues that a well-regulated standing army is superior to every militia and alone can defend a civilised nation, so a professional army is not to be replaced by armed citizens.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: In his digression on the corn trade Smith argues that ordering dealers to sell at a 'reasonable price' in a dearth turns scarcity into famine and that unrestrained freedom of trade is the best remedy.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Smith makes the administration of justice and the defence of society the sovereign's own duties, not tasks for private companies.

production-for-use.rationale: Britannica builds capitalism on private property, the profit motive and market competition, so replacing profit as the purpose of production contradicts it.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Hessen treats the charge that mill owners were exploiters as based on ignorance and defends profit and rivalry as the engines of widely diffused benefit.

property-fundamental.rationale: Hessen names the right to own private property, held as legitimate and defended by the state, as the basic premise of the system; Smith calls property in one's own labour the most sacred and inviolable.

public-ownership.rationale: Britannica defines capitalism as private ownership of most means of production, and Smith writes that no two characters seem more inconsistent than trader and sovereign.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Hessen argues that regulation accumulated since the eighteenth century is hard to repeal and that giant corporations are fully consistent with capitalism, so strict regulation is not part of the case.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Smith argues that the state would do best to deal equally and impartially with all religious sects and let every man choose his own priest and religion.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Smith's account holds that every man should be allowed to choose his own priest and religion as he thinks proper.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Hessen states that the pursuit of self-interest is the basic premise of the system and is morally defensible and legally legitimate.

self-ownership.rationale: Smith holds that the property every man has in his own labour is the original foundation of all other property and the most sacred and inviolable.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Smith says a statesman who tried to direct private people in how they employ their capitals would assume an authority no person or council could safely hold.

state-harmful.rationale: Hessen says the state exists to protect individual rights, and Smith assigns the sovereign the duties of defence, justice and certain public works.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Smith holds that giving domestic produce a monopoly of the home market is almost always a useless or hurtful regulation; Hessen likewise says protected U.S. producers stagnated behind tariff barriers.

taxation-theft.rationale: Smith's Book V treats revenue raised by the sovereign through taxation as necessary to pay for its duties of defence, justice and public works.

total-state.rationale: Hessen says the state exists to protect individual rights and that economic activity should not be regulated by government as socialists propose; Smith limits the sovereign to three duties and leaves private people free to direct their own capital and labour.

trade-surplus.rationale: Smith's Book IV rejects the mercantile doctrine of the balance of trade, in which a country gains by exporting more than it imports.

unions-run-economy.rationale: Hessen and Britannica describe the economy as run by individuals and firms competing in markets, not by organised bodies of workers.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: Smith argues that liberal rewards of labour encourage industry and that an advancing economy raises wages above bare subsistence.

missingStatements.text: Antitrust laws that break up large companies do more harm than good.
missingStatements.rationale: The Econlib article argues antitrust law has often suppressed cost cutting and price cuts and that large firms are consistent with capitalism.

missingStatements.text: Political freedom cannot last without economic freedom.
missingStatements.rationale: Hayek and Friedman, as reported in the Wikipedia article, argued that economic freedom is a requisite of political freedom and that central control accompanies repression.

notes: Rules-7 pass. The earlier answers rested on Wikipedia and on a broad mixed-economy reading; each is now stated by Hessen, Britannica or Smith, or nulled. Themes searched in Smith (Books I-V, full text) and Hessen: trade and tariffs, colonies, interest, price controls, property, taxation, public debt, defence, justice, public works, wages, patents, labour mobility, monopoly and combination, religion, education. Smith and Hessen say nothing on social, cultural, religious, family, immigration, environmental or most constitutional questions, and Britannica gives only a definition, so those statements stay null and the uncertainty rule may exclude the ideology. Britannica's text copy was partial (paywalled), and Econlib and Britannica refused direct fetches, so the Wayback Machine copies are cited. Smith's writings on welfare, labour regulation and progressive taxation point both ways (he calls regulation in the workers' favour 'just and equitable' and a heavier tax on the rich 'not very unreasonable'), so minimum wage, unions and tax-the-wealthy stay null.
